title: Deref and Drop
summary: Following a pointer with *, building MyBox and implementing Deref, deref coercion and its rules with mutability, running cleanup code with Drop, and dropping early with std::mem::drop.

blocks.md:
Two traits make a struct behave like a smart pointer. **`Deref`** lets `*` and method calls go "through" it to the data, so code written for references also works with it. **`Drop`** runs custom code when it goes out of scope, so it can free what it owns.

The **dereference operator** `*` follows a reference to the value:

blocks.explain: `assert_eq!(5, y)` would not compile: you cannot compare a number with a reference to a number. `Box` supports `*` because it implements `Deref`.

blocks.title: Building our own smart pointer
blocks.md: A tuple struct holding one value is enough to see how `Deref` works. (Unlike `Box`, `MyBox` keeps its value on the stack; the point here is the trait, not the storage.)

blocks.explain: `*y` is rewritten by the compiler as `*(y.deref())`: `deref` returns an ordinary reference, which `*` then follows. It returns a reference rather than the value so that `*` does not move the value out of the box.

blocks.title: Deref coercion
blocks.md:
Look at `hello(&m)` again. `hello` takes `&str`, and `&m` is a `&MyBox<String>`. It compiles because of **deref coercion**: when a reference's type does not match a parameter, Rust calls `deref` as many times as needed to make it match, at compile time and at no run-time cost:

`&MyBox<String>` → (`MyBox::deref`) → `&String` → (`String::deref`) → `&str`

Without coercion you would write `hello(&(*m)[..])`. Coercion is why you can pass `&String` to functions taking `&str`, `&Vec<T>` to functions taking `&[T]`, and `&Box<List>` to functions taking `&List`, as in the last lesson.

blocks.title: The three coercion rules
rows: `T: Deref<Target = U>`: mutable can become shared

blocks.title: Never shared to mutable
blocks.md: A shared reference never coerces to a mutable one. The borrowing rules say a mutable reference must be the only reference; converting a `&T` (one of possibly many) into a `&mut U` would break that guarantee.

blocks.title: Deref is for pointers (Programming Rust)
blocks.md: Implement `Deref` only for smart-pointer-like types, whose main job is to give access to a `Target`. Using it to make one type "inherit" another's methods is tempting but confusing: method lookup becomes surprising, and trait bounds do not see through it.

blocks.title: The Drop trait
blocks.md: `Drop` lets you run code when a value goes out of scope: release memory, close a file or a network connection, unlock a lock. `Box` uses it to free its heap allocation. Its one method is `drop(&mut self)`:

blocks.output:
CustomSmartPointers created.
Dropping CustomSmartPointer with data `other stuff`!
Dropping CustomSmartPointer with data `my stuff`!
blocks.explain: Variables are dropped in the **reverse** order of their creation, so `_d` goes first. Each struct's fields are dropped after its own `drop` runs.

blocks.title: Dropping a value early
blocks.md: You cannot call `c.drop()` yourself: Rust would then call it again at the end of scope, a **double free**. The compiler refuses with error E0040, "explicit destructor calls not allowed". To clean up early, for example to release a lock before the scope ends, call **`std::mem::drop`**, which is in the prelude as `drop`:

blocks.output:
CustomSmartPointer created.
Dropping CustomSmartPointer with data `some data`!
CustomSmartPointer dropped before the end of main.
blocks.explain: `drop` is an ordinary function that takes ownership: `pub fn drop<T>(_x: T) {}`. The value moves into it and is dropped when that empty function returns. Ownership guarantees `c` cannot be used, or dropped, again.

blocks.title: Predict the drop order
blocks.md: Before running, write down the order of the `drop` lines. Then run it and compare. Consider: reverse declaration order, a value moved into a function, a value moved into a vector, and shadowing (the old value lives until the end of scope).
hints: `b` is dropped at the end of `take`, right after `take got b`.
At the end of `main`: the second `a`, then `v` (its elements in order: v1, v2), then the first `a`.

blocks.title: A guard that counts and cleans up
blocks.goal: Implement Deref, DerefMut and Drop for a wrapper type, and rely on deref coercion.
blocks.behavior:
`pub struct Tracked<T> { value: T, log: Rc<RefCell<Vec<String>>>, name: String }` wraps a value and records events in a shared log (the `Rc<RefCell<...>>` is explained in the next lesson; just use it as shown in the starter).
- `pub fn new(name: &str, value: T, log: &Rc<RefCell<Vec<String>>>) -> Self` records `"create <name>"`.
- `Deref<Target = T>` and `DerefMut`, so `*t`, `t.len()` and `&t` passed as `&T` all work.
- `Drop` records `"drop <name>"`.
- `pub fn total_len(items: &[&str]) -> usize` (the tests pass `&Tracked<String>` values through deref coercion).

examples.output: 2, and the log is ["create x", "drop x"]

hints: Store `Rc::clone(log)` in the struct so it can log in `drop`.
`impl<T> DerefMut for Tracked<T> { fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut T { &mut self.value } }` (requires `Deref` too).
blocks.solution_explain: In `total_len(&[&x, &y, "f"])`, each `&Tracked<String>` is coerced twice, through `Tracked::deref` and `String::deref`, to `&str`. `v.push(3)` works through `DerefMut`. The drop log confirms reverse order and that `drop(a)` runs the destructor immediately.

points: `Deref` makes `*` and method calls work through a smart pointer; `*x` is `*(x.deref())`.
Deref coercion converts `&Wrapper` to `&Inner` automatically, as many steps as needed.
Mutable can coerce to shared, never the other way.
`Drop::drop` runs at the end of scope, in reverse creation order.
Use `drop(value)` to clean up early; calling the method directly is not allowed.

terms.def: The trait that customizes the * operator and enables deref coercion.
The compiler automatically converting &T to &U through Deref implementations to match a parameter type.
The trait whose drop method runs when a value goes out of scope.
A function that takes ownership of a value and so drops it immediately.
Freeing the same memory twice, a serious bug that Rust prevents.
